This is the first stop in the framework-py tour. Each cell is short and says what to
look for. The notebooks are meant to run in order, 01 to 07, because later ones use
data that 02 adds to the catalog.

## Start every notebook with scaffold()

`scaffold()` finds the project root, loads `.env` and the settings, records the run in
`framework.db`, puts `functions/` on the import path, and runs `scaffold.py`. Look at the
messages under the cell and the root path it returns.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import framework as fw

root = fw.scaffold()
root
```

The working directory is not changed. Quarto runs this notebook from `notebooks/`, yet
Framework still resolves every project path from the root.

```{python}
import os

print("cwd: ", os.getcwd())
print("root:", fw.project_root())
print("framework-py", fw.__version__)
```

`project_path()` builds a path from the root, like R's `project_path()` and
`here::here()`. `Path("outputs/tables")` here would look under `notebooks/`.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

print(fw.project_path("outputs", "tables", "bp_by_visit.csv"))
print(Path("settings.yml").exists(), fw.project_path("settings.yml").exists())
```

## Project status

`status()` prints one overview: the Framework version, project type, git, AI files, the
package manager, and whether each configured folder exists yet. This project sits inside
the `framework-test-projects` repository; the git lines name that repository and count
only this project's own commits and changes.

```{python}
fw.status()
```

`project_info()` returns the same folders as a DataFrame. Folders marked `False` are
created the first time something is saved there.

```{python}
info = fw.project_info(verbose=True)
info
```

The project name and type ride along in the DataFrame's `attrs`.

```{python}
info.attrs
```

## Reading settings

`settings()` looks up a value by dot-notation key. A one-part key is looked up in
`directories` first, so `"notebooks"` returns the notebooks folder.

```{python}
print(fw.settings("notebooks"))
print(fw.settings("directories.outputs_figures"))
print(fw.settings("scaffold.notebook_format"))
print(fw.settings("no.such.key", default="(missing)"))
```

`settings.yml` points at split files under `settings/`. `settings_read()` merges them
in, so the connections from `settings/connections.yml` appear as one section.

```{python}
config = fw.settings_read()
sorted(config)
```

```{python}
config["connections"]["databases"]
```

Settings can have environment sections. `FW_CONFIG_ACTIVE` (or R's `R_CONFIG_ACTIVE`)
picks one, merged over `default`. This project has only `default`, so asking for
`production` gives a `SettingsWarning` and the default values.

```{python}
fw.settings_read(environment="production")["project_name"]
```

## Writing settings

`settings_write()` replaces one section, or the whole file. To keep the real settings
untouched, this cell writes to a copy in a temporary folder. `scaffold` lives in the
split file `settings/scaffold.yml`, so the values are merged into that file. Look at the
comment added first: it survives the write, and `true` stays a YAML boolean.

```{python}
import shutil
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

sandbox = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
shutil.copytree(root / "settings", sandbox / "settings")
shutil.copy(root / "settings.yml", sandbox / "settings.yml")

split = sandbox / "settings" / "scaffold.yml"
split.write_text(split.read_text().replace(
    "  seed:", "  # The seed used when seed_on_scaffold is on\n  seed:"))

fw.settings_write(
    {"seed": "2026", "seed_on_scaffold": True},
    settings_file=sandbox / "settings.yml",
    section="scaffold",
)
print(split.read_text())
```

## Values from .env

Every project has a `.env` file, ignored by git, for credentials. Settings refer to its
values with `env("NAME")` or `env("NAME", "fallback")`. `scaffold()` loaded the file into
`os.environ`; empty values are skipped, so the blank placeholders stay unset.

```{python}
print((root / ".env").read_text())
print("POSTGRES_PORT =", os.environ.get("POSTGRES_PORT"))
print("POSTGRES_HOST =", os.environ.get("POSTGRES_HOST"))
```

This cell shows an `env()` reference resolving in the sandbox copy. The value comes
from the environment, with the fallback when it is missing.

```{python}
fw.settings_write(
    {"study_label": 'env("STUDY_LABEL", "Fictional BP cohort")'},
    settings_file=sandbox / "settings.yml",
    section="options",
)
print(fw.settings("options.study_label", settings_file=sandbox / "settings.yml"))
os.environ["STUDY_LABEL"] = "Set from the environment"
print(fw.settings("options.study_label", settings_file=sandbox / "settings.yml"))
del os.environ["STUDY_LABEL"]
```

## Small helpers

`now()` gives an ISO 8601 timestamp in the same format as R's `framework::now()`.
`capture_output()` collects whatever a block prints, which helps with chatty model
summaries.

```{python}
print(fw.now())

with fw.capture_output() as captured:
    fw.status()
captured.lines[:4]
```

## Creating projects

Framework creates projects from layers: Framework's defaults, your defaults, and the
choices you pass. `tools_available()` lists the tools a Python project can turn on.

```{python}
fw.tools_available()
```

`spec_resolve()` merges layers into one spec, and `spec_check()` lists problems (an
empty list means it is valid). Look at the directories a quarto-workflow project gets.

```{python}
resolved = fw.spec_resolve(
    [{"type": "project", "language": "python", "scaffold": {"workflow": "quarto"}}],
    name="sandbox-project",
)
print(fw.spec_check(resolved.spec))
resolved.spec["directories"]
```

`project_create(headless=True)` builds a project from a spec without git or the project
registry. It goes into the temporary folder, so nothing here changes.

```{python}
created = fw.project_create(resolved.spec, sandbox / "sandbox-project", headless=True)
sorted(p.name for p in created.iterdir())
```

`adopt()` turns an existing folder into a Framework project without moving anything.
It proposes a role for each subfolder; `yes=True` accepts the proposal. Look at how it
mapped `data/raw`, `code`, and `figures`.

```{python}
legacy = sandbox / "old-analysis"
for sub in ("data/raw", "code", "figures"):
    (legacy / sub).mkdir(parents=True)

fw.adopt(legacy, yes=True)
fw.settings("directories", settings_file=legacy / "settings.yml")
```

`new()` is the everyday way to start a project (the same as `fw new NAME --lang python`
on the command line). It runs `git init` and registers the project in your global
settings (except in a temporary folder, as here), so it is off by default. Set
`RUN_NEW = True` to try it; the project goes into the temporary folder.

```{python}
RUN_NEW = False

if RUN_NEW:
    path = fw.new("tour-demo", sandbox / "tour-demo", type="project",
                  workflow="quarto", offline=True, interactive=False)
    print(sorted(p.name for p in path.iterdir()))
```

`project_add_directory()` creates a folder and records it under `extra_directories`.
It edits `settings.yml`, so this runs on the sandbox project.

```{python}
fw.project_add_directory(created, "interviews", "Interview transcripts", "inputs/interviews")
fw.settings("extra_directories", settings_file=created / "settings.yml")
```

## Preparing a fresh clone

`bootstrap()` prepares a cloned project: it creates missing folders, makes sure `.env`
exists and is ignored, and installs packages. `packages=False` skips the install. Look
at the to-do list: it names empty `.env` values that the settings refer to with
`env()`. This project's settings use none, so the list is empty.

```{python}
result = fw.bootstrap(root, packages=False)
result.todo
```

```{python}
shutil.rmtree(sandbox)
```
